description:
We are a team of three in the Manila virtual event, entering Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Our developers cover the data and the web application.

We have room for one more person who writes clear English and can put together slides or a short video. You do not need satellite experience.

We work online in Philippine time for the whole weekend of 14-15 November.
summary: From 2003 to 2025, the January–May fire seasons of the Philippines' eight El Niño years had a median of 40,431 satellite fire hotspots, 2.4 times the 17,012 of the other fifteen years. The rise grows from north to south: the regions' median is 1.7 times in Luzon, 2.7 in the Visayas and 3.0 in Mindanao, and the 63 provinces with enough fires to test range from Aurora (0.9 times) to Zamboanga del Sur (7.7 times). Siklab hotspot calendar, designed for provincial fire officers (Bureau of Fire Protection), DENR forestry offices and local disaster risk reduction and management offices, shows for any province, region or drawn area, month by month since 2003, when it burned, how El Niño seasons compare and, where there are enough fires, the range past El Niño seasons give for January–May 2027. It joins NASA's MODIS and VIIRS records, whose raw counts jump 9.71 times at the 2012 switch, into one record that typically lands within about 10% of a region's yearly total on years the conversion never saw. These numbers describe past seasons, not a forecast, and El Niño years are also less cloudy, so satellites see more of what burns.
details:
What it does. For the whole Philippines, any of 17 regions or 87 province-level areas, or a box the user draws on a NASA map, and any period from January 2003, the application shows:

  • the El Niño response of every province and region: a map of how many times more hotspots the eight El Niño fire seasons (January–May) had than the other fifteen, 2003–2025, a panel for the selected area with both medians, the range and a chance test in plain words, and El Niño years marked on the calendar and the yearly chart;
  • an outlook for January–May 2027 if El Niño holds, as PAGASA expects: for the country, every region and the 63 provinces with enough fires, the median and range of its past El Niño seasons (country: 40,431 hotspots, from 31,825 to 56,760) beside the usual season without El Niño (17,012), with its test on past seasons; a range from past seasons, not a forecast model;
  • a strip of three numbers for the selected area: its El Niño ratio, the share of the year's hotspots in its three busiest months in a row, and the step at 2012 in the harmonised and the raw record;
  • a summary in plain words of the chosen place and period (how many hotspots, when the year burns, the busiest and quietest years, and how the latest month compares with a usual one), with a short explanation for readers who are not scientists;
  • a burning activity calendar: one cell per month, coloured by the number of hotspots on one common scale or by how far each month sits above or below its average (two colour-blind-safe ramps), with months that lack a week or more of satellite data marked;
  • the same calendar in 3D, optional and closed by default: one column per month, taller for more hotspots and coloured as in the calendar, seen with the oldest or the newest year in front;
  • the selected month against the same month in every other year: count, difference from the historical median, mean, and rank;
  • a province map with its own control (El Niño response, hotspots per 100 km² over the period, or the end month against its average), with a ranked list and a table of all 87 provinces; clicking a province opens its calendar;
  • when the year burns (median month and the middle half of years) and which years burned most, with the typical error of the converted MODIS years marked;
  • fire intensity at the hotspots: the fire radiative power of the VIIRS hotspots added up by month, and the average per hotspot by year, with El Niño years marked;
  • day by day: the end month and the two months before it, one bar per day on the same scale as the calendar, against a usual day;
  • a chart that shows what harmonisation changes: raw MODIS, converted MODIS and VIIRS side by side;
  • downloads: monthly analytics (CSV), every hotspot behind the numbers for the search (CSV, with a weight that puts it on the common scale), and the calendar, the map and each chart as images (SVG);
  • a link to every view (the page address keeps the place, period and colours) and a feedback link that opens an issue on GitHub;
  • for a first visit, four ready-made views to start from, each section headed by a question with a one-sentence answer computed from the data, and plain-word definitions of hotspot, MODIS, VIIRS, harmonised, El Niño and fire radiative power;
  • for scientists, a closed "For scientists" note on each section (definition, units, years, filter and the file that holds the numbers), and on the method page a six-line summary, a data dictionary with NASA's product names (MCD14ML, VNP14IMGML, VJ114IMGML and their near-real-time versions), and how to cite the work and rebuild it from a named commit.

The 7-slide demo is also a web page: https://rvbcosme.github.io/siklab-hotspot-calendar/demo . The source code, data pipeline and validation are public: https://github.com/RVBCosme/siklab-hotspot-calendar

El Niño response by province: January–May hotspots in the eight El Niño years against the other fifteen, 2003–2025 (grey: too few fires to tell). Country: 2.4 times.

Outlook for January–May 2027 if El Niño holds: in the eight past El Niño seasons (red), the country had 31,825 to 56,760 hotspots, median 40,431. Predicting each past El Niño season from the others missed by a median of 21.5%, against 37.2% when El Niño was ignored. A range from past seasons, not a forecast.

Every view is summed up in plain words, for readers who are not scientists.

The calendar for Benguet, January 2003 to November 2026, one cell per month on one VIIRS scale.

February 2024 in Benguet: 692 hotspots, 2nd busiest February of 24, against a median of 53.

Where it burned, 2003 to November 2026: hotspots per 100 km² by province. Click a province to open its calendar.

A box drawn on a NASA GIBS map: 11,407 hotspot detections from 2003 to November 2026, about 16,839 on the VIIRS scale.

How it works.

  1. We take NASA FIRMS standard-quality hotspots for the Philippines: MODIS (Terra and Aqua) 2000–2025, VIIRS Suomi NPP 2012–2025 and VIIRS NOAA-20 2018–2025, and 2026 (1 January to 14 November) from the FIRMS area API, standard quality to July (VIIRS) or August (MODIS) and near real time after.
  2. We drop detections FIRMS flags as an active volcano or offshore, and low-confidence detections, with the same rule for both sensors. Not every hotspot is a fire: Mayon and Taal appear in the record.
  3. We place every hotspot in its region and province (geoBoundaries).
  4. VIIRS is the reference scale, because it continues on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 after MODIS ends. For each region, k = VIIRS hotspots ÷ MODIS Aqua hotspots over 2012–2020, on days both satellites delivered data. Aqua passes at the same time of day as Suomi NPP, so k reflects the sensors rather than the daily fire cycle; 2021 onward is left out of the fit because Terra and Aqua no longer hold their orbits and their crossing times have drifted since. Months before February 2012 are MODIS Aqua × k; later months are VIIRS. Days Suomi NPP missed, and every day from 2 November 2026, when Suomi NPP stopped, come from NOAA-20.
  5. Counts are summed by month. Nationally k is 9.8; by region it runs from 7.9 (Mimaropa) to 25.1 (NCR).
  6. The outlook for January–May 2027 is the median, lowest and highest January–May total of the past El Niño seasons, for the country, each region and each province with enough fires. Fire intensity adds up the fire radiative power FIRMS reports for each VIIRS hotspot.

How we know it works. We fixed the tests before the first run.

  • Leaving each year of 2012–2020 out in turn, converted MODIS predicts a region's yearly VIIRS total with a median error of 10.0% (146 region-years), against 90.4% without conversion and 13.0% with one national factor.
  • Single months are less certain (median error 33.4%), so we tell users to read seasons and years, not one month's exact number.
  • The busiest month of the year is the same in both records in 75% of region-years, and within one month in 94%.
  • In 2021–2025, after the orbit drift, the yearly error rises to 21.1%. The calendar uses MODIS only before 2012.
  • NOAA-20 and Suomi NPP differ by a median of 4.8% on a region's yearly total (2018–2025), so the record can continue on NOAA-20 after Suomi NPP stopped on 2 November 2026.
  • Across the change of sensor: the average year 2012–2016 against 2007–2011 is 9.71 times in the raw stitched record, 1.00 in the harmonised record and 1.02 for MODIS Aqua alone, the one satellite that flew through both periods. Region by region the harmonised step differs from MODIS Aqua's own by a median of 4%; the weak spots are NCR (57%) and Bicol Region (25%). The conversion is not exact, but the tenfold step is gone. This is a consistency check, not an independent test: 2012–2016 lies inside the years the factor was fitted on, so the held-out test above is the one that counts.
  • El Niño: in a one-sided permutation test (2,000 random choices of 8 of the 23 years), 7 choices gave a national ratio at least as high (chance probability 0.004). Of 63 provinces with enough fires to test, 41 had more than twice the hotspots in El Niño seasons and 53 have a chance probability under 0.05, where about 3 would by chance. Six of the eight biggest national seasons were El Niño years.
  • The 2027 outlook, tested on past seasons: predicting each of the eight El Niño seasons from the other seven (their median) missed the country's total by a median of 21.5%, against 37.2% when El Niño was ignored (the median of all other seasons). In 46 of 63 provinces the El Niño seasons were the closer guess.
  • What 2026 shows about its limits: January–May 2026, not an El Niño season and outside the record the outlook was built from, had 28,399 hotspots, inside the range of past seasons without El Niño (9,724 to 41,758) but far above their median (17,012); in 49 of 63 provinces the usual season without El Niño was no better a guess for 2026 than the median of all seasons. A busy season can come without El Niño, so the outlook is a range, not a promise.
  • Against reports on the ground: Benguet's three worst January–May fire seasons in our calendar are 2010, 2024 and 2019, the three surges named in local news. The 2010 season comes from converted MODIS and still ranks with the VIIRS years.

Limits we state on the site. A hotspot is not a fire, and no detection does not mean no fire: FIRMS carries no cloud information. Provinces use their region's factor. Metro Manila's factor rests on few fires, and about half of its hotspots are industrial or other static heat sources rather than vegetation fires. From August 2026 the near-real-time data cannot flag offshore detections. El Niño years are less cloudy, so satellites see more of what burns: the El Niño ratio mixes more burning with better visibility, and the record holds only eight El Niño seasons. The calendar describes the past and does not forecast. The 2027 outlook holds only if El Niño holds; it rests on eight seasons, so even by chance a new season falls outside their range about 2 times in 9, and it cannot know 2027's weather, land use or fire control. Fire intensity (fire radiative power) uses VIIRS only, from February 2012: MODIS measures it over larger pixels, so its values are not comparable and are not used, and each value is a snapshot at the satellite's pass, not the energy a fire released.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve. The brief asks for a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Designed for provincial fire officers (Bureau of Fire Protection), DENR forestry offices and local disaster risk reduction and management offices, the calendar gives one comparable number per month since 2003 and shows which provinces' fire seasons have risen most in past El Niño years, and the range those years give for January–May 2027 if El Niño holds. The method is a few hundred lines of open code that any country can re-run from FIRMS files and its own boundary files.

Tools. JavaScript (Node.js) for the data pipeline, with no dependencies; Observable Framework (with Observable Plot, Inputs and D3) for the static web application; Leaflet with NASA GIBS imagery for the custom-area map; GitHub Pages for hosting; GitHub Actions to rebuild on every change.

Built during the hackathon. Everything in this project was made within the hackathon, between the 09:00 start on 14 November and the deadline on 15 November 2026 (Manila time): the data downloads, the pipeline, the validation tests, the web application, the demo and this page. The repository's first commit is at 13:07 on 14 November.

Before the event. Before the start our work was research and logistics: we read the challenge, the rules, the forum and the documentation of NASA's FIRMS files. Two things from that period should be known. On 10 November, before we had read the organisers' guidance on planning (discussion 1872), our AI assistant wrote a text outline of a possible approach and a list of build options, with no code, no design assets, no interface sketches and no data; we set both aside on 11 November and planned the build after the start. On 11 November a forum Navigator had written that NASA's data is public and there is no need to wait for the hackathon to access it (discussion 1925), and the assistant read the first and last few hundred bytes of three 2025 Philippine FIRMS files to learn their column format; nothing was saved or processed. On 14 November the organisers said that downloading data before the start is not permitted (discussion 2011), so we state both here and on the site's Sources page.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI). We used Claude Code (Anthropic), with the Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 models, an AI coding assistant.

  • Before the hackathon: research and fact-checking on the challenge, the NASA data and the rules, and logistics. No code. On 10 November it also wrote a text outline of a possible approach and a list of options, which we set aside on 11 November (see 'Before the event').
  • During the hackathon: it read the 2026 guides and the forum, downloaded the FIRMS files, wrote the data pipeline, the validation tests and the web application's code, drafted the text of the site and of this page, and took the screenshots of the live application used in the demo and on this page. A second AI reviewer read the code independently; its findings were checked against the data before anything was changed. The assistant proposed an approach drawn from the brief, the challenge expert's forum reply on monthly data and published work (Chen and others, 2026); the Team Owner reviewed it and confirmed it for the team. The El Niño comparison, the permutation test and the check against a single satellite were suggested by the assistant (the El Niño theme first as a research topic before the event) and computed from the harmonised record during the hackathon. The Team Owner chose to include them on 15 November and accepted the assistant's recommendations for the tagline, the smallest area tested for El Niño, the three provinces featured and the named users. On 15 November, at the Team Owner's request for forecasts and for 3D, fire-intensity and daily views, the assistant designed and built the El Niño outlook for January–May 2027 (a range from past El Niño seasons, with its test on past seasons) and those three views.
  • What people did: the Team Owner made each open decision (which MODIS satellite to convert, Metro Manila's factor, how the data is kept current, the project name, the disclosure above) and pushed every change to the public repository. The numbers were checked with recounts run by the AI assistant; the tests and their results are on the method page.
  • No AI-generated images, video or audio are used; the only images are screenshots of the application's own pages. AI-written code and data are marked as such in the repository README, on the site's Sources page, in a note at the top of each code file and page, in the data files' metadata (meta.json, validation.json, elnino.json, seam.json, heldout.json, outlook.json) and in each page's HTML metadata.
